cases.title: The Rana Plaza audit: TÜV Rheinland and Phantom Apparel
cases.point: The site of the Rana Plaza building in Savar, outside Dhaka, where Phantom Apparel Ltd ran one of the garment factories.

lenders.name: TÜV Rheinland AG (Germany), through TÜV Rheinland India Pvt. Ltd. (foreign company)
lenders.role: Audited Phantom Apparel Ltd in the Rana Plaza building on 16, 17 and 18 June 2012 under the Business Social Compliance Initiative (BSCI), report BL-18/12. The audit was commissioned by a BSCI member company that the complaint does not name.

cases.conditions: No lender and no loan conditions. What the money bought was a certificate: a BSCI social audit report is what lets a factory keep selling to BSCI member buyers. TÜV Rheinland's own marketing, quoted by ECCHR, calls such reports "a passport for the world market".

companies.name: TÜV Rheinland AG
companies.role: Parent company; respondent in the complaint
companies.desc: German testing, inspection and certification company, 25,900 staff and revenue of 2.71 billion euros in 2024 (Wikipedia).

companies.name: TÜV Rheinland India Pvt. Ltd.
companies.role: Carried out the June 2012 social audit of Phantom Apparel
companies.desc: Indian subsidiary of TÜV Rheinland that performed the BSCI audit.

companies.name: Phantom Apparel Ltd
companies.role: The audited garment factory inside Rana Plaza
companies.desc: Bangladeshi garment maker, one of the factories in the Rana Plaza building.

cases.community: The audit rated the labour part of its assessment as needing improvement and set a mandatory corrective action plan, said no child or young labour was identified, and recorded the building as of "good construction quality, duly approved". Ten months later, on 24 April 2013, Rana Plaza collapsed. The ECCHR complaint states 1,134 people died and around 1,800 were injured; ECCHR's case page gives more than 1,130 killed and more than 2,500 injured, and the OECD Watch summary of the complainants' filing gives 1,138 dead including at least 39 children and 2,500 injured. The complainants set out what they say the audit missed: child workers, some aged 13, and hours for 14-year-olds that interfered with schooling; incomplete workers' registers; machines placed closer together than the law allows, reconstructed from survivors' sketches; no valid building permits for the added floors and industrial use; and workers who did not know of the BSCI complaint mechanism or of their right to leave a dangerous workplace.
cases.killed_note: The collapse of Rana Plaza on 24 April 2013 killed 1,134 people and injured about 1,800 by the figures in the ECCHR complaint. None of the sources opened here ties those deaths to TÜV Rheinland. The June 2012 engagement was a social audit; the company says it was not tasked with assessing the building's structural integrity, and its own press release states it was fully cleared of any liability in connection with the 2013 accident. The toll is therefore recorded here but not counted against the company.
cases.outcome: In July 2015 ECCHR and partners complained to BSCI seeking disclosure of TÜV Rheinland's audit contract and report; BSCI representatives acknowledged a need to clarify auditors' liability and sanctions. In May 2016 ECCHR, survivors and partner organisations filed with the German NCP. The NCP offered mediation, finding the issues warranted further consideration, and both sides accepted. It proposed three elements for an agreement: a common understanding of what social audits can do, a moderated multi-stakeholder dialogue on social audits, and a humanitarian gesture by the respondents that both sides agreed could not be read as an admission of guilt. The parties did not reach agreement. The NCP's final statement of 26 June 2018, shared with the parties on 5 July 2018, recommended a dialogue among audit firms, standard setters, brands, factories and trade unions on the transparency of audit reports and on whether factory owners should pay for their own audits, and pointed to steps audit firms could take already, such as stronger involvement of worker representatives.
cases.whole: The audit produced a report, not a change in the factory. Part B was rated as needing improvement with a mandatory corrective action plan, the report recorded that earlier problems with workers' registration had been resolved on 30 October 2012, and it described the building's construction quality as good. Production continued. TÜV Rheinland reports no figures of its own on what the audit achieved at Phantom Apparel; the only self-reported claim found is its general description of audit reports as a passport to export markets.

cases.title: Logbaba gas project and the Ndogpassi neighbourhoods
cases.point: The Ndogpassi natural gas production unit in Douala III, the Logbaba project's processing site, with the Ndogpassi I, II and III neighbourhoods around it.

lenders.name: Victoria Oil and Gas plc (United Kingdom), through Gaz du Cameroun S.A. (foreign owner)
lenders.role: Wholly owns Gaz du Cameroun, which holds 57% of the Logbaba project and operates it. RSM Production Company holds 38% and Cameroon's Société Nationale des Hydrocarbures 5%.

cases.conditions: No outside lender was found; the money was the operator's own, under a concession in which the state oil company holds 5%. The only conditions on the record are the ones the UK NCP later found unmet: no system to engage the local population, and no contingency plan for preventing or controlling serious environmental and health damage from the operations.

companies.name: Victoria Oil and Gas plc
companies.desc: UK-registered oil and gas company whose main asset is the Logbaba field in Douala.

companies.name: Gaz du Cameroun S.A.
companies.role: Operator of the Logbaba gas and condensate field
companies.desc: Victoria Oil and Gas's Cameroonian subsidiary; it piped gas 34 km to four industrial hubs in the Douala area and had about 128 employees in 2017, 97% of them Cameroonian.

cases.community: 100Reporters found that during construction the company's trucks damaged community water wells. In March 2012 the company dug a replacement well, spending about $25,000; Chief Antoine Tebu said it was not drilled deep enough to reach clean water, and residents described a foul smell and yellow staining. One resident, Frank Tchinda, 23, said: "You would have to be blind to not see that this water is bad." The company and the government said tests at the Pasteur Centre found the water acceptable. The complainants' own survey, recorded by the UK NCP, found 81.70% of respondents had experienced noise from the site and 31.60% complained of odours, and they alleged vibrations had cracked the walls of 23 houses, supplying a proximity map and photographs of soil erosion. Victoria Oil and Gas admitted that on one occasion in September 2017 it failed to warn the local community before flaring. Compensation for houses inside the safety zone was assessed by a commission set up by the Senior Divisional Officer for Wouri; the company said its subsidiary was not part of that commission.
cases.ecosystem: Pasteur Centre reports supplied by the complainants described the water quality as "unsatisfactory and mediocre". The environmental consultant the UK NCP commissioned concluded that none of the documents provided made a compelling case for assigning responsibility to the site, while also finding that the company had left itself open to complaints by not setting a detailed water-quality baseline.
cases.suppression: 100Reporters reports that soldiers of Cameroon's Rapid Intervention Battalion (BIR) were posted at the facility from late 2013. Chief Tebu and a resident, Alain Tedom, 28, described beatings of moto-taxi drivers and their passengers and moto-taxis being barred from the area. On 4 July 2016 a BIR soldier kicked in the door of a garage near the plant, threatened the employees and tried to stab an office worker; the incident was reported to the authorities and to Gaz du Cameroun without response.
cases.outcome: The UK NCP accepted the case on 20 December 2018. Both sides accepted mediation, held one meeting on 30 January 2020, then told the NCP they were pursuing an agreement outside the process; in May 2020 they said they could not reach one, and the NCP began a further examination on 7 May 2020. Its final statement of 22 October 2022 determined that the company did not meet Chapter II paragraphs 7 and 14 on meaningful stakeholder engagement and self-regulatory systems, or Chapter VI paragraphs 5 and 6 on contingency planning and improving environmental performance: materials were not provided in an accessible language, the local population was not given enough time in consultation, and platform meetings were cancelled without notice. It found the company did meet its obligations under the disclosure, human rights and employment chapters and several other environment paragraphs, and found no infringement of the rights to water, to a healthy environment or to decent housing because the link to the site was not established on the evidence available. It recommended the company build engagement systems, keep improving environmental performance and maintain contingency plans, and said it would report back in September 2023.
cases.whole: Production started in December 2011. Offshore Technology records output of 14.59 million standard cubic feet a day from two wells, original proven and probable reserves of 209.6 billion cubic feet of gas and 2.93 million barrels of condensate, about 202.3 billion cubic feet and 2.83 million barrels remaining as of June 2016, gas piped 34 km to four industrial hubs around Douala, condensate sent to the Sonara refinery at Limbe, and a $40 million two-well drilling programme. The figures for what the project gave the neighbourhood are the company's own, reported to the UK NCP and not independently checked: about 128 employees in 2017, 97% of them Cameroonian, $176,000 invested in local staff training since 2011 and a further $165,000 in training under its contract with the state oil company.

cases.confidence_note: The damaged wells, the replacement well and the beatings by soldiers posted at the plant are documented by 100Reporters, outside the complaint. The pollution itself is not established: the UK NCP's own consultant found the documents did not make a compelling case for assigning responsibility to the site, and the company and the government cite Pasteur Centre tests finding the water acceptable, while the complainants cite Pasteur Centre reports calling it unsatisfactory and mediocre. The UK NCP found non-compliance on engagement and on environmental management systems but no infringement of the rights to water, health or housing. The soldiers were state forces; no source opened here records who requested their deployment.

cases.title: La Platosa mine and the Ejido La Sierrita contract
cases.point: The La Platosa silver, lead and zinc mine, standing on land held collectively by the Ejido La Sierrita de Galeana.

lenders.name: Excellon Resources Inc. (Canada), through Excellon de México S.A. de C.V. (foreign investor)
lenders.role: Leased 1,100 hectares of ejido land under a temporary occupation contract signed on 6 April 2008 and mined La Platosa through the dispute. Red TDT records that from 2008 to 2012 the company met the contract's money clauses but not its social and environmental ones.

cases.conditions: The conditions here were the community's, written into the land contract, not a lender's. The 6 April 2008 temporary occupation contract covered 1,100 hectares for 5.5 million pesos a year adjusted annually for inflation, and required a water treatment plant, hiring preference for ejido members, ejido administration of the workers' canteen and of ore transport, school scholarships and a social fund. Four years earlier, in 2004, the company had taken 27 hectares for 30 years for a single payment of 1.2 million pesos (Proceso). Red TDT records that only the rent, the social fund and the scholarships were delivered, and that on 11 March 2011 the company explored outside the 1,100 hectares without the ejido assembly's authorisation.

companies.name: Excellon Resources Inc.
companies.role: Owner and operator of the La Platosa mine
companies.desc: Canadian mining and exploration company; its 2016 annual information form describes it as focused on silver, lead and zinc on a 20,947-hectare property in northeastern Durango, with its principal office at 20 Victoria Street, Toronto.

cases.community: The ejido assembly voted on 8 July 2012 to blockade the mine entrance, and more than seventy landowners did so, after the company cancelled a 6 July meeting that followed nearly eight months of attempts to settle the breaches. On 11 July 2012 MiningWatch Canada reported that Excellon had threatened the landowners and their legal advisers with criminal proceedings and judicial action, calling the blockade illegal and saying state and federal governments would intervene within 24 to 48 hours. On 29 August 2012 about 100 federal police, soldiers, state police and Mapimí municipal police tried to break up the protest, citing a labour inspection of the mine; the protest carried on and the company resumed normal operations. On 24 October 2012, at about 6:30 in the morning, around 250 men from a mining union, brought from Zacatecas and Chihuahua and carrying sticks and stones, cleared the protest camp; the ejido's account, set out by Red TDT, says Excellon's director of operations ordered the camp torn down and burned using mine machinery, and a criminal complaint alleges mine personnel tried to run protesters down with heavy machinery. MiningWatch Canada visited the demolished camp in December 2012. By November 2016, Proceso reported, the company had not paid the rent for three years and had not stopped mining.
cases.suppression: The 29 August 2012 police and army operation to clear the protest; the destruction and burning of the protest camp on 24 October 2012; and the detention, in November 2013, of six community members and relatives of ejidatarios in the days before a court hearing - Héctor Pacheco four days before, and Omar Pacheco, Adolfo Gómez Chareo, Julio Orona, Luis Orona and Ricardo Calderón two days before. Red TDT describes these detentions as arbitrary.
cases.outcome: In November 2012 the Mexican NCP closed the complaint, finding the issues material but not substantiated and citing Excellon's unwillingness to take part in any mediation; the complainants said the threshold for acceptance was unreasonably high and that the Canadian NCP appears not to have been involved at all. In 2011 Canada's Office of the Extractive Sector CSR Counsellor had received a complaint on the same facts, carried out an investigation including a field visit, and concluded the request should go straight to structured dialogue; Excellon withdrew before dialogue began. The ejido went to court instead: on 4 September 2012 it sued for rescission of the contract, restitution of the land and damages (file 683/2012, Tribunal Unitario Agrario del Distrito Sexto, Torreón). Evidence was heard on 23 January 2014. On 7 August 2014 the Juzgado Tercero de Distrito en La Laguna granted an amparo filed on 18 December 2013 (case 2489/2013), ordering the agrarian tribunal to issue a new ruling recognising the ejidatarios' rights and holding that the withheld rent caused the ejido community irreparable harm; the company appealed. A criminal complaint for ecological damage filed on 18 December 2012 produced no investigation. As of 30 November 2014 the tribunal had still not released the rent and the contract remained in force; in November 2016 the ejido filed a further amparo over the delay, seven months after the case had been sent for judgment, and no ruling had issued.
cases.whole: Excellon's own figures for Platosa output are 1.2 million ounces of silver, 7.5 million pounds of lead and 10.1 million pounds of zinc in 2014; 0.8 million ounces of silver, 4.4 million pounds of lead and 7.4 million pounds of zinc in 2015; and 0.8 million ounces of silver, 4.4 million pounds of lead and 5.6 million pounds of zinc in 2016. These are self-reported in the company's annual information form. Of what the 2008 contract promised the ejido, Red TDT records the rent, the social fund and the scholarships as delivered and the water treatment plant, the hiring preference and the ejido-run canteen and ore transport as not; by 2016 the rent had stopped as well.

cases.confidence_note: The court record is outside the complaint: a federal district court in La Laguna granted the ejido's amparo on 7 August 2014 and held that the withheld rent irreparably harmed the community, and Proceso, a Mexican national magazine, reported the unpaid rent and the stalled agrarian case in November 2016. The camp's destruction rests on the ejido's criminal complaint as set out by Red TDT, a Mexican human rights network, together with MiningWatch Canada's visit to the site in December 2012; no police report or court finding on it was opened here. Excellon's own answer was not obtained: the Business and Human Rights Resource Centre lists a company response dated 29 September 2013, but the page opened does not reproduce its text, so the company's position on the camp and the water treatment plant is not recorded. The Mexican NCP found the issues not substantiated, which is a decision on the complaint and not a finding on the facts. The sources also place the land differently: MiningWatch puts the Ejido La Sierrita in Tlahualilo municipality, while the mine's coordinates fall in Mapimí near Bermejillo.

cases.title: PT Panarub, Tangerang: the adidas shoe factory
cases.point: Tangerang, the city in Banten where PT Panarub's shoe factory operates; the sources opened here name the city but not a street address.

lenders.name: adidas-Salomon AG (Germany) (foreign buyer)
lenders.role: Sole customer: the Worker Rights Consortium records that PT Panarub made athletic shoes, including soccer cleats, exclusively for adidas-Salomon. adidas asked the WRC in January 2004 to assess the factory and agreed to share the cost of full legal compliance, including paying a higher rate per shoe.

cases.conditions: There was no lender. The conditions attached to the orders were the buyer's own code: adidas's Standards of Engagement and its membership of the Fair Labour Association, which the German NCP's draft statement praised. The WRC found the factory out of compliance with Indonesian law on overtime, on contractors' wages and on health and safety while those orders were running.

companies.name: adidas-Salomon AG
companies.role: Sole buyer of the factory's output; respondent in the complaint
companies.desc: German sportswear company, named Adidas-Salomon AG after it bought the Salomon Group in 1997 (Wikipedia).

companies.name: PT Panarub
companies.role: The factory; named in the complaint as the company in violation
companies.desc: Indonesian shoe manufacturer with roughly 10,000 workers in 2004, making athletic shoes only for adidas-Salomon.

cases.community: The Worker Rights Consortium assessed the factory in March and April 2004 and published its findings in September 2004. Cleaning-service workers, employed through a contractor, typically worked about 69 hours a week for 629,000 rupiah ($67.95) a month, below the Tangerang minimum wage for a 40-hour week, and their overtime went unpaid; the factory disagreed and did not pay back wages, though it said it would move to two shifts and require contractors to pay the legal minimum. Most production workers were expected to work about two hours of overtime a day, which the WRC found was effectively mandatory - "Mandatory overtime is not allowed under Indonesian law" - and pre-shift production meetings of 15 to 20 minutes were unpaid. Workers handling glues and solvents had inadequate gloves and weak ventilation; hotmelt operators had burns with no hot water or soap to wash; hotpress workers breathed rubber fumes; the waste area had no chemical safety data sheets; trimming machines had no finger guards until the factory fitted them. There was no active registered health and safety committee until a 17-member one was set up. The WRC also found ten named supervisors treating workers abusively, and workers with illnesses possibly linked to chemical exposure pushed into resignation or dismissed. Timothy Connor's 2002 report records 8,000 workers at the time, up to 40% of them on six-month contracts, and that in August 2000, when 600 contract workers' terms ended, nearly all were rehired but all thirty who had joined the Perbupas union were told they were no longer needed.
cases.suppression: In September 2000 Perbupas organised a strike joined by most of the factory's 8,000 workers over unpaid legal overtime rates, menstrual leave and allowances, and management agreed on 12 September not to fire or intimidate those involved. On 23 April 2001 the union's secretary, Ngadinah Binti Abu Mawardi, was arrested and held in Tangerang prison, charged under articles 160 and 335 of the criminal code, a colonial-era provision long used against labour protest. Connor records the Jakarta Post reporting on 25 May 2001 that the arrest followed a complaint by a Panarub executive who told police she had masterminded the four-day strike and put the company's losses at 500 million rupiah. She was released on 23 May 2001 and acquitted on both charges on 30 August 2001; on her return she was moved to the human resources department, away from the production line, and her requests to go back were refused. The WRC found management systematically favouring the rival SPN union over Perbupas in access to new employees, union leave and office space, declining to recognise about 300 workers who had switched unions while still deducting SPN dues, and transferring four Perbupas warehouse officers in February 2003 after they raised workplace concerns; three were dismissed and reinstated on 1 September 2004.
cases.outcome: The Austrian NCP referred the complaint to the German NCP, which accepted it on 10 February 2003 and held two meetings with the parties. Before the second, it circulated a draft statement praising adidas's Standards of Engagement and its Fair Labour Association membership but making no determination on whether labour rights violations at adidas's suppliers had occurred. The Clean Clothes Campaign refused to discuss a draft before adidas answered its four proposals for action; adidas commented on them but rejected any concrete steps. The German NCP issued a statement in September 2004 after the parties failed to agree on a course of action. Separately, adidas commissioned the WRC assessment in January 2004, agreed with most of its findings and recommendations and said it would share the cost of compliance; on supervisor abuse, adidas and the factory rejected the WRC's recommended remedies and issued final warnings and an apology instead, which the WRC accepted.
cases.whole: The factory kept running and kept its single customer. The WRC counted roughly 10,000 workers in 2004, against 8,000 in Connor's 2002 report, up to 40% of them on six-month contracts. What changed in the two years around the complaint came in pieces and mostly from the WRC process rather than the NCP: finger guards fitted to trimming machines and verified, a 17-member health and safety committee established, three dismissed union officers reinstated on 1 September 2004, a promise of two shifts and legal minimum wages for contractors' staff. adidas's undertaking to share the cost of full legal compliance, including a higher price per shoe, is the company's own statement reported by the WRC; no later verification of it was found here.

cases.title: PT Nikomas Gemilang, Serang: Nike's Pou Chen factory
cases.point: The PT Nikomas Gemilang shoe complex at Kibin in Serang regency, Banten, about 60 km west of Jakarta.

lenders.name: Nike, Inc. (United States) (foreign buyer)
lenders.role: Main customer of the factory. Connor's 2001 report for Global Exchange asked Nike to send representatives to meet Nikomas workers and commit to letting them organise without retribution, and to set up a confidential route for workers to report threats; his 2002 report says the requests had been ignored.

lenders.name: Pou Chen Corporation (Taiwan) (foreign owner)
lenders.role: Owns the factory. Connor records it as Nike's largest sport shoe supplier in 2002, with other large plants in China and Vietnam; its arm Yue Yuen began operating at the Serang site in 1993 (Merk).

cases.conditions: No lender and no loan conditions; the outside money was the Taiwanese owner's investment and the buyers' orders. The only conditions on the record are Nike's own code of conduct and its Fair Labour Association membership, which the US NCP cited when it closed the complaint.

companies.name: Nike, Inc.
companies.desc: American athletic footwear and apparel company, described as the world's largest supplier of athletic shoes and apparel (Wikipedia).

companies.name: Pou Chen Corporation
companies.desc: Taiwanese contract manufacturer of athletic and casual footwear, making shoes for Nike, Adidas, Converse and others (Wikipedia).

companies.name: PT Nikomas Gemilang
companies.role: The factory; named in the complaint as the company in violation
companies.desc: Pou Chen's largest Indonesian shoe plant: more than 24,000 workers in 2002 (Connor) and about 68,000 by 2022, 75 to 80% of them women (Merk).

cases.community: Connor's 2002 report records more than 24,000 workers at the plant, making shoes for both Nike and adidas. Workers who organised a pay demonstration on 17 and 18 December 1999 were pushed out: one of them, Julianto, was taken into an office and told, in front of an Indonesian soldier, that he would be attacked by hired thugs if he did not stop organising, and was then approached repeatedly in the street by strangers warning that his life was in danger if he did not resign; another worker came home to find his house ransacked by a local gang. By April 2000 all twenty workers who had played a key part in organising the demonstration had resigned. Workers told Connor the factory had a history of hiring soldiers for security and local thugs to intimidate organisers, and that reporting problems got workers branded as troublemakers, mocked by supervisors or moved to harder and more dangerous sections. Jeroen Merk's 2022 field study found the same pattern two decades on: at least three national unions had tried and failed to set up branches since 2002, the workers who organised a 2002 strike resigned under threat, local strongmen were mobilised to guard the factory during the 2013 wage protests, and the dominant SPN union has never negotiated wages, according to the workers he interviewed. On the money, Merk records that in January 2012 the factory agreed to pay about $1 million in overtime owed to 4,500 workers, some 600,000 unpaid hours over two years, in a practice reported to have run for 18 years; job applicants, he found, commonly paid recruiters one to two months' wages. Asked about organising at the plant, Emelia Yanti of the union federation GSBI told him: "It is very, very difficult at this factory."
cases.suppression: On 21 March 2001 Rakhmat Suryadi, a union official at the factory, was attacked by a number of men with machetes in front of the plant on his way to work. He suffered head and leg wounds, needed 18 stitches in the back of his head, spent a week in hospital and could not work for a month. His attackers said nothing and made no attempt to rob him. The attack came a month after he had been quoted in the Indonesian newspaper Kompas describing labour abuses in Nike contract factories. Local unions and human rights organisations told Connor that several men were arrested over the attack and confessed, saying a local official had paid them. After the attack many workers who had been meeting to discuss their rights stopped doing so. Earlier, the twenty organisers of the December 1999 demonstration were forced out by threats of violence.
cases.outcome: The Clean Clothes Campaign, its Austrian partner and Global Exchange filed on 5 September 2002. The Austrian NCP passed the case to the US NCP, which closed it, saying the information available did not indicate its involvement was needed and that Nike's conduct was being effectively addressed by other means, pointing to the company's participation in the Fair Labour Association. That is a decision on the complaint, not a finding on what happened in Serang. The parallel complaint against adidas, which also sourced from this factory, went to the German NCP and ended in September 2004 without agreement. The unpaid overtime was settled a decade later, in January 2012, for about $1 million covering 4,500 workers.
cases.whole: The plant grew through and after the dispute: from more than 24,000 workers in 2002 to about 68,000 by 2022, three quarters of them women, on a site Pou Chen's Yue Yuen arm had been running since 1993. Nike had 140,000 workers at 14 contract factories in Indonesia by 2011, by the figures its own monitoring supplied to the Associated Press. What the complaint asked for did not arrive: Merk found no successful independent union branch at the factory in the twenty years after 2002, and the only documented payout to workers is the January 2012 overtime settlement, about $1 million for 4,500 workers against roughly 600,000 hours worked and not paid over two years.

cases.confidence_note: The pattern of union suppression at this factory is recorded outside the complaint by Jeroen Merk's peer-reviewed 2022 field study, and the January 2012 overtime settlement he reports was first reported by the BBC; that BBC report was not opened here, so the figures are given as Merk states them. The machete attack and the 1999 intimidation come from Timothy Connor's 2002 report, which is also the report the complaint was based on. Who ordered the attack on Rakhmat Suryadi is not established: Connor records that most of the workers interviewed suspected Nikomas managers, but also that even if a factory was involved it may not have been Nikomas, since Suryadi had supported union activity at the nearby PT Spindo Mills as well. The Nikomas branch leader of the SPTSK union told Connor in January 2002 that wages and conditions at the plant were good and that there was no repression of union rights, which contradicted the confidential testimony of sixteen workers interviewed in July 2001 and January 2002. No response from Nike or Pou Chen to these specific accounts was found in the sources opened. The Associated Press report of 2011 is cited only for Nike's Indonesian workforce figures; the abuse it documents was at other Pou Chen and contractor plants, not at Nikomas.

drops.why: Nothing outside the complaint ties Atlas Copco, an equipment and personnel supplier, to the evictions, killings or cyanide pollution attributed to Ashanti Goldfields at Obuasi; the only non-complaint document found, the Swedish NCP's statement, records the company's role as limited, and the company named in violation, AGC, was operating in its own country.

Same event and same gap as the Atlas Copco complaint: no source outside the complaint links Sandvik's supply of mining equipment and staff to the harm at Obuasi, so test 1 fails even though ActionAid's 2006 field report documents the harm itself.

No source outside the complaint documents the harm: the Dutch NCP's January 2025 follow-up on the related Shell complaint states that the events are the notifier's claims which it did not verify, the Korean NCP closed the case without examining the facts, and no court record, inspection report or newspaper account of the land occupation, waste discharge or armed security at Aminigboko was found.
The same event filed against the Korean parent; dropped for the same reason, no documentation of the harm outside the complaint and the NCP papers.

The surveillance and detention of Uyghurs in Xinjiang is documented far outside the complaint, but UBS's link to it is not: the only account of its ties to Hikvision is the complainants' own research (about US$6.36 million of investment products at the end of 2019, plus nominee shareholding), the Swiss NCP excluded the custodian role from scope and accepted the case only on passive investment, and nothing outside the complaint ties the bank to what happened on the ground.
